claim: Upstash Box bills only active CPU hours (memory free, storage $0.10/GB-month), such that an idle agent sandbox waiting on an LLM response costs nothing on the compute meter once paused; the published worked example shows a box using 10% of one core for an hour costs $0.01 versus $0.20 for 100% of two cores for an hour.
stance_target: idle agent sandbox cost can be driven to near-zero via active-only billing, giving a concrete dollar figure for idle-vs-active cost ratio
quoted_support: An idle box pauses and stops billing active CPU, so a worker that waits for a model response costs nothing on that meter... a box that uses 10% of a single core for one hour costs $0.01, and the same hour at 100% of two cores costs $0.20.

claim: A snapshot fan-out pattern (prepare and snapshot one base environment, then restore N worker sandboxes from it) allows a 3-worker fleet to be provisioned, dependencies-included, in 4.2 seconds total, versus a cold single-sandbox creation measured at 2.1 seconds -- demonstrating that fleet-scale sandbox provisioning latency does not scale linearly with worker count when snapshotting is used.
stance_target: snapshot-based provisioning mitigates the latency cost of spinning up large concurrent agent fleets, which is the counterpart tradeoff to aggressive auto-kill/scale-to-zero policies
scope_conditions: Upstash Box SDK, measured single-run timings, Node runtime, small size
quoted_support: Three workers restored, ran and confirmed the install in 4.2 seconds in total... Box.create(): 2102 ms

claim: Shared checkouts across concurrent coding agents produce test failures unrelated to the agents' actual tasks because agents interfere with each other's dependency installs and working trees; per-agent sandbox isolation is necessary (not merely a security nicety) for a 100+-agent fleet to produce trustworthy results.
stance_target: one-sandbox-per-agent is a scaling requirement, not just an isolation/security requirement, for a software factory architecture
scope_conditions: general claim about concurrent coding agents sharing a filesystem
quoted_support: Twenty agents on one machine are not twenty workers, they are twenty ways to break the same checkout... One shared checkout cannot host a fleet of agents. A fleet of sandboxes can.
